RIYA SHANKAR STOOD ON AN EMPTY street in Des Moines at 6:57 PM before a one-story suburban house with a gabled roof, checkered with red bricks. An oversized garage took up most of the façade.
She wore a faded green sweater with yoga pants and worn-out sneakers. A fruit platter rested awkwardly in her left hand as she pulled a ticket stub from her pocket and checked the time again.
*Echo Sounds Presents: Intimate Concert.*
A gift to herself for turning twenty-five in five hours. Which was, she realized, a thing you did when there was no one else to give you one.
Throughout her life, she had wanted two things: to not end up like her mother or her father.

Her earliest memories of her mother were of a woman already somewhere else. Every night, her mother sat alone on the living room floor, picking at her food in the blue glow of the television. When Riya sat beside her, she would begin listing the grievances with her father, the things she never got to do in life because of the loveless marriage, a broken record that Riya knew by heart. As a child, she would listen for as long as she could before quietly slipping away, understanding, without being told, that her mother needed an audience more than a daughter.

Her father, on the other hand, only came home once every two weeks. She would hear the gate and feel her stomach tighten. His love had a grading system. An A in Mathematics meant a rare hand on her shoulder. Anything less and the house would fill with a particular kind of silence before the eruption of insults. The one she most remembered was: *I sit in an office I hate every day so you can have a future.* She would sit very still and think: *if I had just gotten one more question right*.

Riya had figured it out early: excellence was armor. Score high enough and her father smiled. Score even higher and the girls who whispered behind her back in the hallway would show up at her desk before exams, suddenly friendly, needing her help. But by the time she reached college, she couldn't remember what it felt like to read something just because she wanted to.

What she wanted now was embarrassingly simple. A career that gave back what the grading system had robbed of her—the joy of learning as a child. And someone who grabbed her face and kissed her against the kitchen counter on a Tuesday night, Joni Mitchell playing somewhere, not caring who else was around.
And yet, she would turn twenty-five in five hours with a job she hated, in a city she did not love, and no one to kiss her. Her wants were embarrassingly simple, and yet, seemed maddeningly far away.
She tucked the ticket stub back into her pocket, wondering how long it was appropriate to wait before someone called the cops on her.

When she moved to Des Moines after grad school at CMU, there was so much promise. A salary for the first time in her life after a decade of debt. A bedroom to herself. The pride in her father’s voice when he told relatives from their village in India that his daughter was working in the United States of America.
It felt like she had arrived.
But no one warned her about the shrinking.

It crept in slowly, so slow and sinister that she hadn’t noticed the walls closing in. Over time, her world shrank into a ten-minute daily commute to the Horizon Mutual office, evenings at the park reading beneath a sycamore tree, and long hours at the public library charting ideas for an education platform she was too afraid to build. Soon enough, the only person who said her name with enthusiasm was the barista at the local coffee shop, *Bean There, Done That.*

She wasn’t a recluse. She still showed up to work on time each day. She talked to her co-workers about optimizing car insurance funnel conversions. But she had begun to disappear inside her own life. Even her roommate Preeti felt like a stranger. The two of them coexisted like passengers pressed against each other on a long-haul flight—polite nods and a shared talent for avoiding eye contact.

Maybe it was Horizon Mutual’s fault, full of employees who were married with children and had no time for a restless woman in the midst of a quarter-life crisis. Or her tiny room, which had just enough space to fit a bed and a folding table. She tried to blame the job, the apartment, even her manager who made her the scapegoat for everyone’s errors. But the quiet followed her everywhere.
“Here for the show?”
Riya looked up, startled.
A pale, thin woman with big, beady eyes and a lip ring emerged from the backyard door carrying an overstuffed trash bag.
“Oh. Um, yeah?”

“You’re just a liiiittle early.” The woman chuckled and hoisted the bag over her shoulder. She pushed open the wooden gate to the backyard. “Walk to the end and make yourself home, hon. I’ll be back in a minute.”

Riya tiptoed on the damp grass to the backyard. Still, no concert. Just a bare garden with brown leaves and a lone microphone stand at the far end. If this went well, she’d walk away with a friend. If not, she’d wake up another year with no one to celebrate her birthday with. No matter what, tonight, she promised to not leave early.
The woman walked back in, wiping her hands on cargo pants, and thrust her hand forward. “I’m Ana. What’s your name, early bird?”
“It’s Riya. Like Leah, with an R. Um, I got some fruits for people.” She held out the platter.
“Aren’t you sweet?” Ana took it. “Thanks, hon.”
“Is the concert not at seven?”
Ana laughed. “You’re not a concert-goer, are you?”
Riya shook her head, biting her lips.

“Let me tell you three things about concerts, bird.” Ana held up three fingers. “One, never sleep with the lead singer. They smell like patchouli, and they’ll forget your name in five minutes. Two, always show up an hour late or you’ll end up helping the host set up. And three, remember rule number one.”
Riya nodded, her eyes darting over to the tattoo of a fish on Ana’s collarbone.
“Alright,” Ana clapped her hands. “Let’s start setting up the merch tables.”

Thirty minutes later, miraculously, a venue was born. All it took were some tables, chairs, a scattering of plush throwaway pillows, and fairy lights strung between the tall oak trees framing the yard. It helped that the sun pulled the curtains down on the sky just as the bulbs flickered to life. They smiled at each other. Maybe Ana would become her new friend.
Three tall, handsome men who could’ve been mistaken for indie models walked in just as they finished taping the last set of bathroom directions onto the walls.
“Ana!”
The man in the wrapped her in a long hug and leaned back, examining the setup.
“Meet little bird a.k.a Riya,” Ana said, pointing. “She helped with the setup.”
“Aren’t you sweet?” He leaned in for a hug.

Riya stiffened before she could stop herself, heat rising to her face at the sudden closeness of a male body. The last person she hugged was her grandfather more than a year and a half ago before she left India.
“Sooo,” he said, turning to Ana. “We need someone at the merch table. Our volunteer bailed.”
Ana’s eyebrows lifted toward Riya.
“Sure, I can do it,” she said quickly.
Ana blew her a kiss. “You’re the best, hon.”
By eight o’clock, the backyard was packed, people crawling out of the house like ants, plastic cups in hand.

Ana was lost in the crowd, floating from one guest to another at the speed of a wasp. Riya stood behind the merch table with an invisible straightjacket around her, arms crossed, nodding to anyone who came by to glance at the tote bags and enamel pins with the commitment of someone killing time at a mall. Everyone seemed to know everyone.
“Hi,” she said to a woman hovering near the table. “Can I help you?”
The woman looked up. “No, thanks.”
She drifted away.
Riya winced under her breath. “Great. I sound like I work at Target.”
Stay, she told herself. Don’t leave early. Whoever came next, she decided, she’d ask where they’re from.
Then, it happened.

It started with the smell of bergamot, followed by a soft ripple of a crowd parting just slightly. Heads turned in sync. Then, the mob exclaimed. Riya rose onto her toes and saw a loose blonde ponytail swinging as he moved through the crowd, pulling a force field with him, hugging people intimately, laughing.

He wasn’t conventionally attractive, not like the band guys with chiseled faces. He wasn’t tall, broad, or Hollywood-handsome. Just shy of five foot ten, he was pale with an average build, but a presence that demanded attention without asking for it. His blonde hair, still damp at the ends, was pulled back casually and paired with a multicolored robe and loose white cotton pants. When he drifted toward the merch table, she straightened her spine.
His eyes held her attention. Big. Piercing. Blue. They seemed to reach straight into her soul as if searching for something she was scared to admit.
“You’re new.” He simply said it, like it was the truest thing in the world.
“Y-yes. How did you know?”
“So am I.” He winked. “We’re the only two people who aren’t performing.”
“Performing?”

He tilted his head toward the crowd. People laughing too loudly, hugging with exaggerated enthusiasm, swaying a little too theatrically to the music. He pointed at a tall, lanky guy laughing with Ana.
“He’s not laughing because it’s funny,” he said. “He’s laughing to perform for her. They all know their roles.” He looked back at her. “We don’t.”

He motioned for her to follow him to a quieter spot. She hesitated only half a second before stepping out from behind the table. He leaned against the fence, studying her. “So,” he said. “Tell me about yourself. But please, don’t tell me your name or what you do.”
“I…” What else could she possibly say about herself?
“What do you want me to say?”
His lips curved. “Anything but your name or what you do.”
She glanced at the fairy lights for emotional support, but found none.
“I memorize quotes,” she said finally.
He raised an eyebrow. “Quotes?”
“From famous people. I know over a thousand of them.”
“See?” He smiled. “I knew there was something interesting about you.”
Riya’s fingers tightened around the hem of her sweater. The way he said it sent a tiny thrill through her.
“Alright,” he said, rubbing his hands. “Hit me with a Roosevelt.”
“Which one?”
Confused, he said, “Uh, Theodore Roosevelt, the former President of America?”
Riya smiled faintly. ‘“Comparison is the thief of joy.’” She didn’t add that she’d memorized it on a night she’d compared herself to everyone she knew.
He nodded, seeming impressed. “David Bowie?”
‘“I don’t know where I’m going from here, but I promise it won’t be boring.’”
He chuckled and shook his head. “How do I know you’re not making these up?”
She tilted her chin slightly. “Go look it up.”
“Alright. Jeopardy style.” He cleared his throat dramatically. “This German poet once said, ‘He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.’”
“Who is… Nietzsche?”
“It’s pronounced *Nee-chuh*, but yeah.”
“Huh.” She tilted her head. “Most people go with Shakespeare or Oprah.”
“I’m just special that way,” he winked.
“Where are you from?” she asked. “I assume it’s not Des Moines?”
“God, no.” He snorted and took a sip. “My heart belongs to San Francisco. Always has and always will.”
She might’ve felt insulted at the jab at her city, except it wasn’t hers either.
“What’s so special about San Francisco?”
His face lit up, as if she’d unlocked something inside him.

“Have you heard of Herb Cain?” he asked. She shook her head. “He’s a famous columnist who once wrote, ‘One day if I go to heaven, I’ll look around and say, ‘It ain’t bad, but it ain’t San Francisco.’’ That’s how I feel about the city. It’s one of the only places that doesn’t just tolerate differences—it worships it. You walk down a street and see a juggler in a business suit, a… a guy on stilts, someone playing piano in a damn laundromat. It’s chaotic, but it’s where I feel most alive and home.”
She nodded slowly, wondering if she’d ever felt that way about any city.
“Can I ask you something?” she asked.
He smirked. “Anything but my name or what I do.”
“Where are you from, originally?”

He turned toward her more fully, like he hadn’t expected that question. His accent was almost inconspicuous, but for her ears. It slipped in only at the edges, curling slightly around certain vowels, making his English sound just a little too crisp, too deliberate.
“North Germany.”
“Do you visit often?”
His face twitched—just slightly.
“No. I have no ties back home.”
“Why?”
He took a sip instead of responding. “Have you thought about how every city can be described in just *one* word?”
She let it go. “Can it?”
“Go ahead. Pick a city.”
“Um, New Jersey?”
“Odd choice, but okay.” He leaned closer. “One word.”
Despite living there for two years during grad school, she’d never let herself explore the city. So she blurted out the first thing that came to mind.
“Patel Brothers.”
He burst out laughing.
“That’s weirdly specific.”
She laughed too. “I know. Also, I cheated. That was two words.”
“Okay, okay, what about Des Moines?”
She looked down at her worn-out sneakers, then up at the sky as if the answer might be written there. Des Moines wasn’t bad. It wasn’t good. It just was. A waiting room with fluorescent bulbs.
“I honestly don’t know,” she said quietly.
He tilted his head. “Why are you in Des Moines?”
“My job,” she said.
“Do you have to be here to do it?”
“Well—“ she stammered, mildly annoyed at his flippant certainty. “I don’t know. I never checked.”
“So, check and leave the city,” he said, taking a sip.
“No thanks. I like it here.”
“Do you?”
His confidence was beginning to grate on her. “Yes. You don’t even know this city.”
“But I know you.”
She felt her chest compress. What was he doing to her? She looked away from his intent gaze, but he kept looking at her.
He leaned in. “You never asked me the one word for San Francisco.”
She looked at him, biting her lip. “What is it?”
He barely paused before answering.
“*Chutzpah*.”
“Hutspah?”
“Chutzpah. It’s Yiddish,” he replied. “It means audacity. Nerve. A kind of boldness you don’t apologize for.”

The last time she had felt anything close to that was at twelve, riding her bicycle freehand through the narrow, muddy streets of her village in India. Her cast had just come off after a broken arm. She’d lifted both hands anyway—palms open to the sky—daring herself to fall. The wind rushed past her as she sped downhill, grinning ear to ear. That girl felt foreign now.
“You should visit.” He studied her. “You don’t belong here. We have a spare room in our community house. We don’t just let anyone in, but I’ll put in a good word for you.”
She wanted to protest, protect the dignity of a city she didn’t care for, but all that came out was a barely audible, “Thank you.”

They stood beneath a lemon tree lit up by fairy lights, the air thick with citrus and damp grass. Riya expected him to toss the paper cup and move on to someone else. But he stayed there, leaning against the fence, and continued to look at her like he had nowhere better to be. She looked away at first, out of reflex. Her eyes flitted from the merch table to the stage where the singers were tuning their guitars, to Ana laughing too loudly at something she couldn’t hear. When it finally returned to him, he was still there. She noticed a dimple that appeared when he almost smiled, and smiled without meaning to. For a brief moment, the world shrank just to the two of them, and nothing else seemed to matter.
Then the band cut through the stillness, announcing they were about to begin, the first chords humming through the yard.
He leaned in, close enough that she felt his breath, his piercing blue eyes gleaming with mischief, spiking her heart rate.
“Now,” he said softly, barely above a whisper, “I actually want to know your name.”
“It’s, um, Riya.” It was absurd, how vulnerable it felt to say something so simple.
“Good to meet you, *um* Riya.”
She laughed awkwardly.
“Riya.” He repeated, slower this time, like testing the shape of it in his mouth.
With a dramatic flourish, he extended his hand, mocking a corporate interview handshake.
“Hello, *um* Riya, I’m Felix.”
She shook his hand, her palm warmer than she’d expected. Without asking, Felix took her phone, keyed in his number, then handed it back. “Message me if you ever come there.”
Before she could respond, the first chords of that night’s performance swelled to life behind them.
Riya smiled at her reflection in the scratched steel walls of the elevator carrying her out of the BART and into her first sight of a city she’d only seen in pictures and movies.
Eight days.

That was all it had taken to pack up her life and move across the country to San Francisco. Her manager had agreed, begrudgingly, to let her work remotely. Company policy was on her side. Her roommate, Preeti, had decided to move out too, and their final week together passed without much fanfare, two presences brushing past each other like ghosts in the hallway, a series of doors opening and closing. After selling all furniture, she was left with two suitcases that bottled her whole life.

San Francisco offered something Des Moines no longer could—anonymity. No one knew her here. She could quit her job, start a company, fall in love, buy a car, speak on a stage, scream in a park, drink alcohol, paint a model, maybe even get a tattoo. Anything she wanted. Today, though, all she wanted was to cook a meal for everyone in the house, make friends in them, and be the *last* to retreat to her room.

The doors were about to open to 18th Street and Mission. She expected the sight of mural-splashed walls, young founders in hoodies scooting on bikes, maybe even to spot the glass spire of the iconic Salesforce tower piercing the skyline.
Her toes tingled. This is it. It was the feeling of *knowing* your life was about to change in mere seconds.
Ten excruciating seconds later, the doors opened to the smell of urine.
